I'm checking the team's claim that no warning fires: with by="desk" on the in-memory engine, the sortedness warning should trigger unless the streaming path is used, so I'm tracing which engine join_asof actually takes.

I'm working out whether the in-memory engine would still route this through the check, and it looks like it would, since the by-group path skips the sortedness check and fires the warning. I'm also starting to compute the physical categorical codes for the "by" column, so I can see what the grouping actually produces.

Now I'm checking the asof join on the physical codes: the left values 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 against right values 3 and 1, which gives "d" for every row in the backward direction and nulls in the forward direction. Then I'm turning to the by="desk" path, where all rows fall into one group and the right-side indices are split across threads.

Each partition gets its own group state, so with five or more threads every left row starts fresh: the first two match "d" and the rest come back null. The answer is the same as a single shared state only when that state still lines up, so the thread count matters here.

I'm working out the streaming path now: with no "by" argument, the streaming engine takes the ungrouped asof route, and the sortedness check passes on the logical categorical values, so I'm tracing what that produces on the physical codes.

I'm checking how the streaming engine would split this input, and the morsel size works out to one row per morsel once there are at least five pipelines. The pruning compares Categorical values lexically, while the kernel itself runs on the physical codes, so I'm looking at whether those two orderings could disagree here.

I'm walking through how the streaming engine would hand off one left row at a time: the binary search on lexical values decides whether more right-side rows are needed, and with the left row "a" the buffer is empty, so the next right row "b" gets pulled in.

I'm stepping through the streaming case for the "b" row: the right buffer holds only "b", so the backward search returns index 0 and that row picks up "b". Then for the next left row, "b", I need another right-side row, so I'm pulling in "d" and checking the physical values 3 against right codes 3 and 1 to see which match.

I'm working through the streaming case for the left row "d": the right side runs out, so the join falls back to the remaining buffered rows, and I'm checking whether pruning after "c" leaves anything that changes the outcome.

Now I'm finishing the streaming trace: the result is ["b","d",None,None,None], which I can explain by noting that one-row morsels decide which right-side rows each left row sees. I'm also checking why sorting by the physical codes makes the frame look unsorted by its logical Categorical values.

So the question is whether the sortedness check and the kernel even agree. Lexically, 'e' sorts after 'd', so the frame doesn't pass the check and raises. The check reads the Categorical values, but the kernel works on the physical codes, so the two orderings can disagree. String and Enum avoid this: strings compare by bytes the same way in both places, and enums sort by their declared order, which here is already a through e. Categories that were added in a, b, c, d, e order line up with that same ordering, so the physical codes match the lexical order in a fresh session.

I'm tracing the root cause to the asof-join key comparison, which runs on the physical codes of a Categorical column. Those codes follow insertion order, while the sortedness check and Categorical ordering are lexical, so the two can disagree. The acceptance test in `_check_asof_columns` allows the key because its physical type is a primitive UInt32.

I'm checking whether the asof-join acceptance test in `_check_asof_columns` actually makes a decision on the by-path and the streaming path, since both pass the physical codes in already. In the by-path the sortedness check is skipped and the key arrives as a UInt32, so the dtype test only sees the physical type there.

I'm checking whether `_check_asof_columns` is the place where the Categorical key gets accepted, since it tests the key with `to_physical().is_primitive()`. I'm also listing which callers reach it: the in-memory ungrouped join, the by-group join, and the streaming ungrouped join.

I'm noticing the helper would accept a Categorical key only because its physical type is a primitive UInt32, so the lexical-vs-physical mismatch slips through. The by-path and streaming callers already hand it the physical codes, so changing the helper alone wouldn't catch those cases; the logical key would have to be passed through instead.

Still writing the dtype checks in `_check_asof_columns`...

I'm checking whether `_check_asof_columns` is the place that accepts the Categorical key, since its `to_physical().is_primitive()` test passes because the physical type is UInt32. I'm also listing its callers: the in-memory ungrouped join, the by-group join, and the streaming ungrouped join, which all hand it physical codes before the check runs.

I'm wondering whether the bug is in `is_sorted` for Categoricals instead, since the team says the check passes on both columns. If it were physical, the loans column would fail, so the lexical check is what's passing, and I'm working out which ordering is actually the wrong one.

I'm checking whether the lexical-ordering decision for Categorical keys is made in the join conversion layer instead of the asof helper, since upstream may have special-cased categoricals there.

I'm going to check whether the idiom for ordering-based operations on Categoricals is to convert them to strings, so I'm searching the repo for `uses_lexical_ordering` and `is_categorical()` checks in sorting and search code.
